title: Your Computer Is Not Magic
description: Discover how computers actually work beneath the glass: an unbroken physical pipeline of Input, Processing, and Output, with optional Storage for later retrieval.

primaryCapability.statement: Trace a simple computer action through input, processing, and output.

secondaryCapabilities.statement: Distinguish the roles of input, processing, output, and storage in everyday computer interactions.
Reason about when information needs to be stored for later retrieval versus existing temporarily during an interaction.

objectives.statement: Trace information through input, processing, and output in everyday computing interactions.
Classify computer interactions according to input, processing, output, and storage.
Distinguish between temporary information during an interaction and information stored for later retrieval.

content.question: When you click a button on a web page or in an app, what actually causes something to happen on your screen?

options.text: The button itself contains the logic and directly changes the screen.
The button sends an input signal to the computer's processor, which runs instructions and produces an output.
The button immediately writes to long-term storage, which then refreshes the display.
The display detects the mouse click directly and draws the reaction.

content.explanation: A button is just an input trigger. It does not perform computation on its own. When clicked, it sends a signal to the processor, which executes instructions and directs the screen to change.

feedback.correct: Correct! The button is merely an input trigger. The processor does the actual work.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The button itself cannot compute anything or change pixels directly. It simply generates an input signal for the processor.

content.title: The Standard Information Pipeline
content.description: Step through the three core stages of computation: Input, Processing, and Output. Watch how data moves forward from an event to a visible result.

config.title: The Standard Information Pipeline
config.description: Step through the three core stages of computation: Input, Processing, and Output.

scenarios.title: Clicking a Button
scenarios.description: Observe how a user interaction moves from the physical mouse click to a visible change on screen.

steps.title: 1. Input: The Physical Event
steps.description: The user presses the mouse button over 'Submit'. The mouse hardware sends an electrical click coordinate signal into the computer.

steps.title: 2. Processing: Instructions Execute
steps.description: The processor receives the click signal, identifies the button, validates the entered form fields, and updates application state.

steps.title: 3. Output: Visual Result
steps.description: The processor directs the graphics system to redraw the screen, rendering a green 'Form Saved Successfully!' confirmation banner.

scenarios.title: Typing a Character
scenarios.description: See how a single keystroke flows across the computer.

steps.title: 1. Input: Key Press
steps.description: You press the 'A' key on your physical keyboard. A scan code signal is sent to the operating system.

steps.title: 2. Processing: Glyph Resolution
steps.description: The computer converts the scan code into character code 65 ('A') and computes the new cursor offset.

steps.title: 3. Output: Render Glyph
steps.description: The monitor refreshes pixels at the cursor location to display the letter 'A'.

interactive.caption: Notice how data flows: Input enters, Processing transforms it, and Output displays the result.

content.title: Trace Familiar Interactions
content.description: Explore how different daily computing actions map across the pipeline. Switch between scenarios to inspect what constitutes Input, Processing, Output, and whether Storage is engaged.

config.title: Trace Familiar Interactions
config.description: Explore how different daily computing actions map across the pipeline.

scenarios.title: Calculating 2 + 2
scenarios.description: When you enter 2 + 2 on a calculator, where does the calculation happen?

mapping.prompt: You type '2 + 2 =' into a calculator app. Which pipeline stage actually performs the arithmetic addition?

choices.rationale: Tapping the buttons sends numbers into the computer, but buttons cannot do arithmetic.
Correct! The processor takes the numbers and executes addition instructions to produce 4.
The display only presents the result after the calculation is already finished.
Basic calculations are held in active memory and shown on screen; they are not saved to disk unless explicitly recorded.

mapping.explanation: The processor performs arithmetic calculations. Input delivers the operands, and Output displays the sum.

scenarios.title: Bookmarking a Web Page
scenarios.description: Identify the stage that allows you to find this page next week.

mapping.prompt: You click the star icon in your browser to bookmark a page so you can reopen it next week after turning off your computer. Which stage ensures the bookmark survives?

choices.text: Input (The mouse click on the star)
choices.rationale: The click only triggers the event; it does not preserve the data.
Processing creates the record in memory, but without storage it would vanish on shutdown.
The yellow star is visual feedback that the action happened, not the persistent storage.
Correct! Storage writes the bookmark record to persistent disk so it survives when the computer is turned off.

mapping.explanation: Storage is the intentional persistence of information to survive beyond the immediate session.

scenarios.title: Typing in a Search Bar
scenarios.description: Map the stages of entering text.

mapping.prompt: As you type letters into a search box, letters immediately appear on screen before you hit Enter. Is long-term storage required for this letter display?

choices.text: No — this is pure Input → Processing → Output in active memory
choices.rationale: Correct! Showing what you typed only requires receiving key events, updating the input buffer in memory, and rendering pixels.

choices.text: Yes — every keystroke must be saved to permanent storage to appear
choices.rationale: Displaying text on screen is output from active memory, not permanent disk storage.

mapping.explanation: Live typing works via the Input → Processing → Output loop. Storage only comes into play if you submit or save the search history.

interactive.caption: Storage is only engaged when data must survive beyond the immediate interaction.

content.title: Active Memory vs. Deliberate Storage
content.text:
When you type in a search box or move your mouse, the computer processes data at blinding speed. But seeing something on your screen does **not** mean it has been saved.

Every computer operation produces temporary intermediate data. If power is lost or you refresh the page without saving, that intermediate state vanishes. **Storage is not step four** of every interaction — it is a deliberate decision to write information to a medium where it persists after the interaction ends.

callout.text: Common Misconception: 'If I can see it on my screen, it's already saved.' Pixels on a screen are just output. Storage only happens when data is explicitly committed to long-term memory.

content.keyTakeaway: Output is immediate and transient; storage is deliberate and durable.

content.prompt: Order the stages that occur when you type a chat message and hit 'Send':

items.text: You press the 'Enter' key on your keyboard (Input)
The app packages your text into a data payload and assigns a timestamp (Processing)
The message is written to database storage so conversation history is kept (Storage)
The chat bubble appears in your conversation window (Output)

content.explanation: Input initiates the sequence. Processing structures the message. In a chat application, persistence (storage) records the chat before/as output renders the new bubble.

feedback.correct: Spot on! The key press (input) triggers packaging (processing), gets stored in chat history (storage), and displays on screen (output).
feedback.incorrect: Remember the sequence: an external action enters first (Input), gets handled by software (Processing), persists in history (Storage), and appears on screen (Output).

content.question: You point your phone's camera at a sunset. The screen continuously shows what the camera sees (viewfinder). Then you tap the circular shutter button to snap the picture. What describes the storage role here?

options.text: Every frame shown on the viewfinder is saved to storage automatically.
The viewfinder is continuous Input → Processing → Output; Storage only occurs when you tap the shutter button to save that specific frame.
The phone screen itself acts as the storage device for the photo.
Photos are never stored; they exist only as light signals inside the camera sensor.

content.explanation: The live preview continuously flows through input (sensor) → processing (color adjustments) → output (screen preview). Storage is only engaged when you explicitly trigger the shutter to persist that specific frame into your photo library.

feedback.correct: Excellent transfer! Continuous preview is pure Input → Processing → Output. Storage only happens when you explicitly command the phone to save.
feedback.incorrect: Look closely at the distinction between previewing and saving: seeing the live scene does not fill your storage. Storage only happens when you take the photo.

content.title: The Machine Demystified
takeaways: A computer is not magic: it executes deterministic steps across an Input → Processing → Output pipeline.
Buttons and UI elements do not 'do the work' themselves; they generate input signals for a processor.
Storage is not a mandatory fourth step in every cycle; it is an intentional act of persistence.
Output (displaying on screen) is transient. Only data explicitly saved to storage survives session end.
nextSteps: In the next lesson, you will see how this pipeline operates across the web: how your browser acts as the client taking input, talking across the network to a server, and rendering web output.
reviewQuestions: What are the three core stages that every computer interaction must pass through?
Why is storage considered an optional or parallel branch rather than a required fourth step?
